title: Keep one line of Marcus
hook: twelve books to himself: death, duty, kindness, the whole

segments.voice: Yesterday, the book's last section: the actor dismissed after three acts. Your line was three acts is a play. Did you let the acts you've had count? Day two hundred twenty-five.

When you finish a long book, what do you actually keep? Usually not the plot. Usually one sentence. One line that stuck to you, that shows up years later when you're stuck in traffic or can't sleep. We've now walked through all twelve books of Marcus Aurelius's notebook, written in Greek and addressed, again and again, to himself. Death, duty, kindness, the whole. Before we leave him, one job. Today, keep one line of Marcus.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU KEEP FROM A BOOK?` → `ONE LINE THAT STICKS.` → `TWELVE BOOKS, ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Let's walk back through the notebook, quickly, like flipping pages. Book one: his debts. From my grandfather, from my mother, from whom I learned. Then time. You've been putting it off, and there is a limit. Do each thing as if it were the last. Live three thousand years or three, and you only lose this moment. Then beauty in the wrong places: the cracked loaf, the split fig. Stand upright, not propped up. The inner retreat, open at any hour. Nature loves change. Like the vine, do good and move on. The mind is dyed by the thoughts you keep. The obstacle becomes the way. A purple robe is sheep's wool dyed in shellfish blood. Don't be turned into a Caesar. What isn't good for the hive isn't good for the bee. You'll meet the future with the same reason you have now. Then a plain one. In George Long's 1862 translation: "Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig." Then: it's not the thing, it's my view of it. A bitter cucumber? Put it down. Of course there are rude people. Stop arguing about what a good person is; be one. Like leaves. Graft back. Kindness is invincible. And three acts can be the play. Notice the four threads that keep returning. Death, used to wake up the present. Duty, the work in front of you. Kindness, even to difficult people. And the whole, the sense of being one small part of something vast. You don't need all of them. You need one.
screen: `DEBTS, AND THE LIMIT OF TIME.` · `UPRIGHT, DYED, THE OBSTACLE.` · `DIG WITHIN. BE ONE.` · `DEATH, DUTY, KINDNESS, THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `KEEP ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your line, and then copy it out. Settle and breathe. Let the lines drift past again. The cracked loaf. Dig within. Kindness is invincible. The obstacle becomes the way. Wait for the one that tugs. Don't pick the wisest. Pick the one you need. Repeat it slowly inside, three or four times, until it feels like yours. After the bell, write it down by hand. The bell holds the time.
Keep one line of Marcus. Twelve books to himself, about death, duty, kindness and the whole; one line is enough to carry. Today's word.
screen: `KEEP ONE LINE OF MARCUS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: keep one line. Today, write your Marcus line by hand, and put it where you'll see it tomorrow morning: a mirror, a wallet, a phone case. Day two hundred twenty-five.

screen: `DAY 225 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KEEP ONE STORY OF RUMI.`

howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius copy out a single line from the Meditations and keep it on a card, a wall or a lock screen, rereading it each morning.
